THE WEIL CONJECTURE. I
by PIERRE DELIGNE

CONTENTS

1. Grothendieck’s theory: cohomological interpretation of L-functions ................................. 273
2. Grothendieck’s theory: Poincaré duality ............................................................. 280
3. The fundamental estimate .................................................................................. 283
4. Lefschetz theory: local theory ............................................................................. 287
5. Lefschetz theory: global theory ............................................................................ 289
6. A rationality theorem ....................................................................................... 294
7. Completion of the proof of (1.7) .......................................................................... 298
8. First applications ........................................................................................... 301

In this article I prove the Weil conjecture concerning the eigenvalues of Frobenius endomorphisms. A precise statement is given in (1.6). I have tried to present the proof in as geometric and elementary a form as possible, and I have included many reminders: only the results of §§ 3, 6, 7, and 8 are original.

In an article following this one, I shall give various refinements of the intermediate results, and applications, among them the “hard” Lefschetz theorem (on iterated cup products by the cohomology class of a hyperplane section).

The text faithfully follows six lectures given at Cambridge in July 1973. I thank N. Katz for allowing me to use his notes.

1. Grothendieck’s theory: cohomological interpretation of L-functions.

(1.1) Let X be a scheme of finite type over Z, let |X| be the set of closed points of X, and, for x∈|X|, let N(x) be the number of elements of the residue field k(x) of X at x. The Hasse-Weil zeta function of X is

(1.1.1)    ζ_X(s) = ∏_{x∈|X|} (1 − N(x)^(−s))^(−1)

(this product converges absolutely for Re(s) sufficiently large). For X = Spec(Z), ζ_X(s) is the Riemann zeta function.

We shall consider exclusively the case in which X is a scheme over a finite field F_q.

For x∈|X|, we shall write q_x rather than N(x). Setting deg(x)=[k(x):F_q], we have q_x=q^deg(x). It is useful to introduce the variable t=q^(−s). Put

(1.1.2)    Z(X; t) = ∏_{x∈|X|} (1 − t^deg(x))^(−1) ;

this infinite product converges for |t| sufficiently small, and

(1.1.3)    ζ_X(s) = Z(X; q^(−s)).

(1.2) Dwork (On the rationality of the zeta function of an algebraic variety, Amer. J. Math., 82, 1960, p. 631-648) and Grothendieck ([1] and SGA 5) proved that Z(X,t) is a rational function of t.

For Grothendieck, this is a corollary of general results in ℓ-adic cohomology (ℓ denotes a prime number different from the characteristic p of F_q). These furnish a cohomological interpretation of the zeros and poles of Z(X;t), and a functional equation when X is proper and smooth. Dwork’s methods are p-adic. For X a nonsingular hypersurface in projective space, they likewise furnished a cohomological interpretation of the zeros and poles, and the functional equation. They inspired the crystalline theory of Grothendieck and Berthelot, which, for X proper and smooth, furnishes a p-adic cohomological interpretation of the zeros and poles, and the functional equation. Building on ideas of Washnitzer, Lubkin created a variant of this theory, valid only for X proper, smooth, and liftable to characteristic zero (A p-adic proof of Weil’s conjectures, Ann. of Math., 87, 1968, p. 105-255).

We shall make essential use of Grothendieck’s results and recall them below.

(1.3) Let X be an algebraic variety over an algebraically closed field k of characteristic p, i.e. a separated scheme of finite type over k. We do not exclude the case p=0. For every prime ℓ≠p, Grothendieck defined ℓ-adic cohomology groups H^i(X,Q_ℓ). He also defined cohomology groups with proper support H_c^i(X,Q_ℓ). For X proper, the two coincide. The H_c^i(X,Q_ℓ) are finite-dimensional vector spaces over Q_ℓ, and vanish for i>2 dim(X).

(1.4) Let X_0 be an algebraic variety over F_q, let F̄_q be an algebraic closure of F_q, and let X be the algebraic variety over F̄_q obtained from X_0 by extension of scalars from F_q to F̄_q. In the language of Weil or Shimura, one would express this situation as: “Let X be an algebraic variety defined over F_q.” Let F:X→X be the Frobenius morphism; it sends a point with coordinates x to the point with coordinates x^q; in other words, for U_0 a Zariski-open subset of X_0 defining an open subset U of X, one has F^(−1)(U)=U; for x∈H^0(U_0,O), one has F^*x=x^q. a) The set X^F of closed points of X fixed by F identifies with the set X_0(F_q)⊂X_0(F̄_q) of points of X defined over F_q. This simply expresses that, for x∈F̄_q, x∈F_q ⇔ x^q=x.

b) Likewise, the set X^(F^n) of closed points of X fixed by the n-th iterate of F identifies with X_0(F_{q^n}).

c) The set |X_0| of closed points of X_0 identifies with the set |X|_F of F-orbits (or φ-orbits) in |X|. The degree deg(x) of x∈|X_0| is the number of elements in the corresponding orbit.

d) From b) and c) one obtains the formula

(1.4.1)    #X^(F^n) = #X_0(F_{q^n}) = ∑_{deg(x)|n} deg x

(for x∈|X_0| and deg(x)|n, x defines deg(x) points with coordinates in F_{q^n}, all conjugate over F_q).

(1.5) The morphism F is finite, hence in particular proper. It therefore induces maps

           F^* : H_c^i(X,Q_ℓ) → H_c^i(X,Q_ℓ).

Grothendieck proved the Lefschetz formula

           #X^F = ∑_i (−1)^i Tr(F^*,H_c^i(X,Q_ℓ));

the right-hand side, a priori an ℓ-adic number, is an integer and equals the left-hand side. Such a formula is reasonable only because dF=0, even at infinity (X is not assumed proper); the relation dF=0 implies that the fixed points of F have multiplicity one.

An analogous formula holds for the iterates of F:

(1.5.1)    #X^(F^n) = #X_0(F_{q^n}) = ∑_i (−1)^i Tr(F^(*n),H_c^i(X,Q_ℓ)).

(1.5.2)    t·d/dt log Z(X_0,t)

           t·d/dt log Z(X_0,t)

hence

(1.5.4)    Z(X_0,t) = ∏_i det(1−F^*t,H_c^i(X,Q_ℓ))^((−1)^(i+1)).

The right-hand side is an element of Q_ℓ(t). The formula states that its Taylor expansion at t=0, a priori a formal series in Q_ℓ[[t]] with constant term one, belongs to Z[[t]] and equals the left-hand side, itself also regarded as a formal series in t. This is Grothendieck’s cohomological interpretation of the function Z.

Our principal result is the following.

Theorem (1.6). — Let X_0 be a nonsingular (= smooth) projective variety over F_q. For every i, the characteristic polynomial det(t·1−F^*,H^i(X,Q_ℓ)) has integer coefficients independent of ℓ (ℓ≠p). The complex roots α of this polynomial (the complex conjugates of the eigenvalues of F^*) have absolute value |α|=q^(i/2).

We first show that (1.6) follows from the apparently weaker result below.

Lemma (1.7). — For every i and every ℓ≠p, the eigenvalues of the endomorphism F^* of H^i(X,Q_ℓ) are algebraic numbers all of whose complex conjugates α have absolute value |α|=q^(i/2).

Proof that (1.7) implies (1.6). — Regard Z(X_0,t) as a formal series with constant term 1, an element of Z[[t]]: Z(X_0,t)=∑_n a_n t^n. By (1.5.3), the image of Z(X_0,t) in Q_ℓ[[t]] is the Taylor expansion of a rational function. This means that, for N and M sufficiently large (at least the degrees of the numerators and denominators), the Hankel determinants

           H_k = det((a_(i+j+k))_(0≤i,j≤M))    (k>N)

vanish. This vanishing holds in Q_ℓ if and only if it holds in Q; therefore Z(X_0,t) is the Taylor expansion of an element of Q(t). In other words,

           Z(X_0,t) ∈ Z[[t]] ∩ Q_ℓ(t) ⊂ Q(t).

Write Z(X_0,t)=P/Q, with P,Q∈Z[t] relatively prime and with positive constant terms. By a lemma of Fatou, the fact that Z(X_0,t) belongs to Z[[t]] and has constant term one implies that the constant terms of P and Q are 1. Put

           P_i(t)=det(1−F^*t,H^i(X,Q_ℓ)).

THE WEIL CONJECTURE. I

By hypothesis (1.7), the P_i are pairwise relatively prime. The right-hand side of (1.5.4) is therefore in reduced form, and

           P(t) = ∏_{i odd} P_i(t)
           Q(t) = ∏_{i even} P_i(t).

Let K be the subfield of an algebraic closure Q̄_ℓ of Q_ℓ generated over Q by the roots of R(t)=P(t)Q(t). The roots of P_i(t) are precisely those roots of R(t) having the property that all their complex conjugates have absolute value q^(−i/2). This set is stable under Gal(K/Q). Hence P_i(t) has rational coefficients. By Gauss’s lemma (or because the roots of P_i, being roots of R(t), are inverses of algebraic integers), it even has integer coefficients. The preceding description of the roots of P_i(t) is independent of ℓ; consequently, P_i(t) itself is independent of ℓ.

The rest of this article is devoted to the proof of (1.7).

(1.8) Grothendieck’s theory gives a cohomological interpretation not only of zeta functions, but also of L-functions. The results are as follows.

(1.9) Let X be an algebraic variety over a field k. For the definition of a constructible Q_ℓ-sheaf on X, I refer to SGA 5 VI. It will suffice to say that:

a) If ℱ is a constructible Q_ℓ-sheaf on X, there is a finite partition of X into locally closed parts X_i such that ℱ|X_i is twisted constant.

b) Suppose X is connected and let x̄ be a geometric point of X. For ℱ twisted constant, π₁(X,x̄) acts on the fiber ℱ_x̄; the fiber functor at x̄ is an equivalence of categories

           (constructible twisted-constant Q_ℓ-sheaves on X) ↦
           ↦ (continuous representations of π₁(X,x̄) on finite-dimensional Q_ℓ-vector spaces).

Such a representation does not, in general, factor through a finite quotient of π₁(X,x̄).

c) If k=C, constructible Q_ℓ-sheaves on X identify with sheaves of Q_ℓ-vector spaces ℱ on X^an such that there is a finite partition of X into Zariski-locally closed parts X_i and, for each i, a local system ℱ_i of free Z_ℓ-modules of finite type on X_i, with

           ℱ|X_i = ℱ_i ⊗_(Z_ℓ) Q_ℓ.

We shall consider only constructible Q_ℓ-sheaves and shall simply call them Q_ℓ-sheaves.

(1.10) Suppose k is algebraically closed, and let ℱ be a Q_ℓ-sheaf on X. Grothendieck defined ℓ-adic cohomology groups H^i(X,ℱ) and H_c^i(X,ℱ). The H_c^i(X,ℱ) are finite-dimensional vector spaces over Q_ℓ and vanish for i>2 dim(X).

For k=C, H^i(X,ℱ) and H_c^i(X,ℱ) are the usual cohomology groups (respectively, with proper support) of X^an, with coefficients in ℱ.

(1.11) Let X_0 be an algebraic variety over F_q, let X be the corresponding variety over F̄_q, and let ℱ_0 be a sheaf of sets on X_0 (for the étale topology). Denote its inverse image on X by ℱ. Besides the Frobenius morphism F:X→X, one then has a canonical isomorphism F^*:F^*ℱ→^{~}ℱ. Here is a description. Regard ℱ_0 as an étalé space over X_0, i.e. identify ℱ_0 with the algebraic space [ℱ_0], endowed with an étale morphism f:[ℱ_0]→X_0, such that ℱ_0 is the sheaf of local sections of [ℱ_0]. The analogous space [ℱ], étalé over X, is obtained from [ℱ_0] by extension of scalars. We therefore have a commutative diagram

                     F
              [ℱ] ───→ [ℱ]
               │ f       │ f
               ↓         ↓
               X ───→    X
                     F

whence a morphism [ℱ]→X×_(F,X,f)[ℱ]=[F^*ℱ], which is an isomorphism because f is étale. Its inverse defines the desired isomorphism F^*ℱ→^{~}ℱ.

This construction generalizes to Q_ℓ-sheaves.

(1.12) Let X_0 be an algebraic variety over F_q, let ℱ_0 be a Q_ℓ-sheaf on X_0, let (X,ℱ) be obtained from (X_0,ℱ_0) by extension of scalars from F_q to F̄_q, and let F:X→X and F^*:F^*ℱ→ℱ.

The finite morphism F and F^* define an endomorphism

           F^* : H_c^i(X,ℱ) → H_c^i(X,F^*ℱ) → H_c^i(X,ℱ).

For x∈|X|, F^* defines a morphism F_x^*:ℱ_(F(x))→ℱ_x. For x∈X^F, this is an endomorphism of ℱ_x. Grothendieck proved the Lefschetz formula

           ∑_(x∈X^F) Tr(F_x^*,ℱ_x) = ∑_i (−1)^i Tr(F^*,H_c^i(X,ℱ)).

An analogous formula holds for the iterates of F: the n-th iterate of F^* defines morphisms F_x^(*n):ℱ_(F^n(x))→ℱ_x; for x fixed under F^n, F_x^(*n) is an endomorphism, and

(1.12.1)    ∑_(x∈X^(F^n)) Tr(F_x^(*n),ℱ_x) = ∑_i (−1)^i Tr(F^(*n),H_c^i(X,ℱ)).

(1.13) Let x_0∈|X_0|, let Z be the corresponding orbit of F in |X|, and let x∈Z. The orbit Z has deg(x_0) elements (1.4). Denote by F_(x_0)^* the endomorphism F_x^(*deg(x_0)) of ℱ_x, and put

           det(1−F_(x_0)^*t,ℱ_0) = det(1−F_(x_0)^*t,ℱ_x).

Up to isomorphism, (ℱ_x,F_(x_0)^*) does not depend on the choice of x. This justifies omitting x from the notation. We shall use analogous notation for other functions of (ℱ_x,F_(x_0)^*).

(1.15) It is sometimes convenient to use Galois language rather than geometric language. Here is the dictionary.

If F̄_q^1 and F̄_q^2 are two algebraic closures of F_q, then (X_0,ℱ_0) over F_q defines, by extension of scalars, (X_1,ℱ_1) over F̄_q^1 and (X_2,ℱ_2) over F̄_q^2. Every F_q-isomorphism σ:F̄_q^1→^{~}F̄_q^2 induces an isomorphism

PIERRE DELIGNE

2. Grothendieck’s theory: Poincaré duality.

(2.1) To explain the relation between roots of unity and orientations, I shall first restate two classical cases in a fanciful language.

a) Differentiable manifolds. — Let X be a differentiable manifold purely of dimension n. The orientation sheaf Z′ on X is the sheaf locally isomorphic to the constant sheaf Z whose invertible sections over an open subset U of X correspond to the orientations of U. An orientation of X is an isomorphism from Z′ to the constant sheaf Z. The fundamental class of X is a morphism Tr:H_c^n(X,Z′)→Z; if X is oriented, it identifies with a morphism Tr:H_c^n(X,Z)→Z. Poincaré duality is expressed with the aid of the fundamental class.

b) Complex varieties. — Let C be an algebraic closure of R. A smooth complex algebraic variety, or rather its underlying differentiable manifold, is always orientable. To orient it, it suffices to orient C itself. This amounts to the choice:

a) of one of the two roots of the equation X^2=−1; it is called +i;

b) of an isomorphism of R/Z with U^1={z∈C | |z|=1}; +i is the image of 1/4;

c) of one of the two isomorphisms x↦exp(±2πix) from Q/Z onto the group of roots of unity in C, which extends by continuity to an isomorphism from R/Z onto U^1.

Let Z(1) denote a free Z-module of rank one whose two-element set of generators is in canonical correspondence with one of the two-element sets a), b), c). The simplest choice is Z(1)=Ker(exp:C→C^*). The generator y=±2πi corresponds to the isomorphism c):x↦exp(xy).

Let Z(r) be the r-th tensor power of Z(1). If X is a smooth complex algebraic variety purely of complex dimension r, the orientation sheaf of X is the constant sheaf with value Z(r).

(2.2) To “orient” algebraic varieties over an algebraically closed field k of characteristic 0, one must choose an isomorphism from Q/Z onto the group of roots of unity in k. The set of these isomorphisms is a principal homogeneous space under Ẑ^* (no longer under Z^*). When one is interested only in ℓ-adic cohomology, it suffices to consider roots of unity whose order is a power of ℓ, and to assume that the characteristic p of k is different from ℓ. Let Z/ℓ^n(1) denote the group of roots of unity in k whose order divides ℓ^n. As n varies, the Z/ℓ^n(1) form a projective system, with transition maps

           σ_(m,n) : Z/ℓ^m(1) → Z/ℓ^n(1) : x↦x^(ℓ^(m−n)).

Put Z_ℓ(1)=lim proj Z/ℓ^n(1) and Q_ℓ(1)=Z_ℓ(1)⊗_(Z_ℓ)Q_ℓ. Let Q_ℓ(r) denote the r-th tensor power of Q_ℓ(1); for r∈Z negative, put also Q_ℓ(r)=Q_ℓ(−r)^∨.

As a vector space over Q_ℓ, Q_ℓ(1) is isomorphic to Q_ℓ. However, the automorphism group of k acts nontrivially on Q_ℓ(1): it acts through the character with values in Z_ℓ^* that gives its action on the roots of unity. In particular, if k=F̄_q, the Frobenius substitution φ:x↦x^q acts by multiplication by q.

Let X be a smooth algebraic variety purely of dimension n over k. The orientation sheaf of X in ℓ-adic cohomology is the constant Q_ℓ-sheaf Q_ℓ(n). The fundamental class is a morphism

           Tr : H_c^(2n)(X,Q_ℓ(n)) → Q_ℓ,

or, equivalently,

           Tr : H_c^(2n)(X,Q_ℓ) → Q_ℓ(−n).

Theorem (2.3) (Poincaré duality). — For X proper and smooth, purely of dimension n, the bilinear form

           Tr(x∪y) : H^i(X,Q_ℓ)⊗H^(2n−i)(X,Q_ℓ) → Q_ℓ(−n)

is a perfect duality (it identifies H^i(X,Q_ℓ) with the dual of H^(2n−i)(X,Q_ℓ(n))).

(2.4) Let X_0 be a proper smooth algebraic variety over F_q, purely of dimension n, and let X over F̄_q be obtained from X_0 by extension of scalars. The morphism (2.3) is compatible with the action of Gal(F̄_q/F_q). If the (α_j) are the eigenvalues of the geometric Frobenius F acting on H^i(X,Q_ℓ), the eigenvalues of F acting on H^(2n−i)(X,Q_ℓ) are therefore the (q^nα_j^(−1)).

(2.5) Suppose, for simplicity, that X is connected. The proof of (2.4) translates as follows into geometric rather than Galois language (cf. (1.15)).

a) Cup product puts H^i(X,Q_ℓ) and H^(2n−i)(X,Q_ℓ) in perfect duality with values in H^(2n)(X,Q_ℓ), which is one-dimensional.

b) Cup product commutes with pullback F^* by the Frobenius morphism F:X→X.

c) The morphism F is finite and of degree q^n: on H^(2n)(X,Q_ℓ), F^* is multiplication by q^n.

d) The eigenvalues of F^* therefore have property (2.4).

(2.6) Put χ(X)=∑_i(−1)^i dim H^i(X,Q_ℓ). If n is odd, the form Tr(x∪y) on H^n(X,Q_ℓ) is alternating; the integer nχ(X) is therefore always even. It follows readily from (1.5.4) and from (2.3), (2.4) that

           Z(X_0,t) = ε·q^(−nχ(X)/2)·t^(−χ(X))·Z(X_0,q^(−n)t^(−1)).

(2.14) Bibliographical notes on §§ 1 and 2.

A) All important results in étale cohomology are first proved for torsion sheaves. The extension to Q_ℓ-sheaves is made by formal passages to the limit. In what follows, for each theorem cited, I shall refer not to a source in which it is proved, but to a source in which its analogue for torsion sheaves is proved.

B) With the exception of the Lefschetz formula and (2.12), all the results in étale cohomology used in this article are proved in SGA 4. For those already stated, the references are: definition of H^i: VII; definition of H_c^i: XVII 5.1; finiteness theorem: XIV 1, completed in XVII 5.3; cohomological dimension: X; Poincaré duality: XVIII.

C) The relation among the various Frobenius elements ((1.4), (1.11), (1.15)) is explained in detail in SGA 5, XV, §§ 1, 2.

D) The cohomological interpretation of Z-functions (1.14.3) is clearly set out in [1]; however, the Lefschetz formula (1.12), for X a projective smooth curve, is used there but not proved. For the proof, one must, alas, refer to SGA 5.

E) The form (2.12) of the Poincaré duality theorem follows from the general result SGA 4, XVIII (3.2.5) (for S=Spec(k), X=X, K=j_*ℱ, L=Q_ℓ) by a local calculation that is not difficult. The statement will appear explicitly in the definitive version of SGA 5. (ii) The image of π₁(U,u) in GL(ℱ_u) is an open subgroup of the symplectic group Sp(ℱ_u,ψ_u).

Lemma (3.3). — Let 2k be an even integer, and write ⊗^(2k)ℱ_0 for the (2k)-th tensor power of ℱ_0. For x∈|U_0|, the logarithmic derivative

           t·d/dt log(det(1−F_x t^deg(x),⊗^(2k)ℱ_0)^(−1))

is a formal series with nonnegative rational coefficients.

Hypothesis (iii) ensures that, for every n, Tr(F_x^n,ℱ_0)∈Q. The number

Lemma (3.4). — The local factors det(1−F_x t^deg(x),⊗^(2k)ℱ_0)^(−1) are formal series with nonnegative rational coefficients.

The formal series log det(1−F_x t^deg(x),⊗^(2k)ℱ_0)^(−1) has no constant term; by (3.3), its coefficients are ≥0; the coefficients of its exponential are therefore also nonnegative.

Lemma (3.5). — Let f_i=∑_n a_(i,n)t^n be a sequence of formal series with constant term one and nonnegative real coefficients. Suppose that the order of f_i−1 tends to infinity with i, and put f=∏_i f_i. Then the radius of absolute convergence of f_i is at least that of f.

4. Lefschetz theory: local theory.

(4.1) Over C, the local results of Lefschetz are as follows.

Let D={z | |z|<1} be the unit disk, let D^*=D−{0}, and let f : X→D be a morphism of analytic spaces. Suppose that

a) X is nonsingular and purely of dimension n+1;

b) f is proper;

c) f is smooth away from a point x of the special fiber X_0=f^(−1)(0);

d) at x, f has a nondegenerate quadratic point.

Let t≠0 in D and let X_t=f^(−1)(t) be “the” general fiber. To the preceding data one associates:

α) specialization morphisms sp : H^i(X_0,Z)→H^i(X_t,Z): X_0 is a deformation retract of X, and sp is the composite arrow

           H^i(X_0,Z) ←^{~} H^i(X,Z) → H^i(X_t,Z);

β) monodromy transformations T : H^i(X_t,Z)→H^i(X_t,Z), which describe the effect on the singular cycles of X_t of “turning t around 0.” Equivalently, this is the action on H^i(X_t,Z), the fiber at t of the local system R^i f_*Z|D^*, of the positive generator of π₁(D^*,t).

Lefschetz theory describes α) and β) in terms of the vanishing cycle δ∈H^n(X_t,Z). This cycle is well defined up to sign. For i≠n,n+1, one has

           H^i(X_0,Z) →^{~} H^i(X_t,Z)    (i≠n,n+1).

For i=n,n+1, one has an exact sequence

           0 → H^n(X_0,Z) → H^n(X_t,Z) →^{x↦(x,δ)} Z
             → H^(n+1)(X_0,Z) → H^(n+1)(X_t,Z) → 0.

For i≠n, the monodromy T is the identity. For i=n,

           Tx = x ± (x,δ)δ.

The values of this sign, of Tδ, and of (δ,δ) are as follows:

           n mod 4             0      1      2      3
           Tx=x±(x,δ)δ         −      −      +      +
           (δ,δ)                2      0     −2      0
           Tδ                  −δ      δ     −δ      δ

Lemma (6.7). — Let K be a finite set of integers different from 1, and let (δ_j) (1≤j≤Q) and (ε_j) (1≤j≤Q) be two families of elements of a field. We argue by induction on Q. The set of integers n such that δ_Q^n=ε_j^n is an ideal (n_j). Let us prove that there is a j_0 such that δ_Q=ε_(j_0). Otherwise the n_j would all be different from 1, and there would be arbitrarily large integers n divisible by none of the n_j and by none of the k∈K. We would then have δ_Q^n≠ε_j^n, contradicting the hypothesis. Thus there is a j_0 such that δ_Q=ε_(j_0). Let us first prove that (7.2) implies (1.7). For X_0 smooth and projective over F_q and i an integer, the following assertion must be proved:

W(X_0,i). Let X be obtained from X_0 by extension of scalars from F_q to F̄_q. If α is an eigenvalue of F^* acting on H^i(X,Q_ℓ), then α is an algebraic number all of whose complex conjugates, again denoted α, satisfy |α|=q^(i/2).

a) If F_(q^n) is an extension of degree n of F_q, and X′_0/F_(q^n) is obtained from X_0/F_q by extension of scalars, then W(X_0,i) is equivalent to W(X′_0,i): extending the scalars amounts to replacing α by α^n and q by q^n.

b) If X_0 is pure of dimension n, W(X_0,i) is equivalent to W(X_0,2n−i): this follows from Poincaré duality.

c) If X_0 is a sum of varieties X_0^α, W(X_0,i) is equivalent to the conjunction of the W(X_0^α,i).

d) If X_0 is pure of dimension n, Y_0 is a smooth hyperplane section of X_0, and i<n, then W(Y_0,i) implies W(X_0,i): this follows from the weak Lefschetz theorem.

To prove the assertions W(X_0,i), we reduce successively:

— by c), to the case where X_0 is pure of some dimension n;

— by b), to the further case 0≤i≤n;

— by a) and d), to the further case i=n;

— by a) and c), to the further case where X_0 is absolutely irreducible.

This case is covered by (7.2).

Theorem (8.2). — Let N be an integer >= 1, let ε : (Z/N)* -> C* be a character, let k be an integer >= 2, and let f be a holomorphic modular form on Γ₀(N), of weight k and character ε: f is a holomorphic function on the Poincaré upper half-plane X such that, for (a b; c d) ∈ SL(2, Z), with c ≡ 0 (N), one has

Lemma (8.7). — Y₀ is smooth away from the inverse image of H₀.

On the affine part, Y₀ = X₀ is étale over A₀ and hence smooth. At infinity, but away from the inverse image of H₀, there are local coordinates (z₁,...,z_n) in which Q = z₁^{-d} (this uses (d,p) = 1). Lemma (8.8). — In an étale neighborhood of a point above H₀, Y₀ is smooth over one and the same normal singular surface.

This time one can find local coordinates in which Q = z₁^{-d}z₂. Indeed, since H₀ is smooth, div(Q)_f is smooth near infinity and meets P₀^∞ transversely. This form is independent of the chosen point and involves only two coordinates, which proves the assertion.

(8.9) It is known that the following procedure (due to Zariski) resolves surface singularities: one alternately normalizes and blows up the (reduced) singular locus. The operations involved commute with étale localization and with taking a product with a smooth space. Zariski’s procedure therefore also resolves the singularities of a space which, like Y₀, is étale-locally smooth over a surface. The resulting resolution of Y₀ is the desired Z₀.
